events.title: Landing: Bradbury Landing
events.text: 6 Aug 2012. Curiosity lands on the Aeolis Palus plain in Gale crater.

events.title: Yellowknife Bay: ancient lake
events.text: Feb 2013. First drill sample (John Klein) shows an ancient freshwater lake environment that could have supported microbes.

events.title: Pahrump Hills: base of Mount Sharp
events.text: Sep 2014. Arrival at the mountain; start of the climb through lake-deposited mudstone layers.

events.title: Vera Rubin ridge
events.text: Sep 2017. A hematite-rich ridge, studied for more than a year.

events.title: Glen Torridon: clay unit
events.text: Jan 2019. Clay-bearing layers seen from orbit; the best-preserved record of water.

events.title: Gediz Vallis: pure sulfur
events.text: 30 May 2024. Curiosity crushes a rock and reveals yellow crystals of elemental sulfur, a first for Mars.

events.title: Boxwork region
events.text: 2025. Mineral ridges 1–2 m tall left by groundwater; ridge and hollow drill samples.

events.title: Today: latest position
events.text: Last reported drive, sol 5073 (NASA MMGIS feed).

sites.title: Water & sulfur feedstock: Gediz Vallis sulfate unit
sites.why: Curiosity found a field of pure elemental sulfur stones (2024) inside the hydrated sulfate layer of Mount Sharp. Hydrated sulfates release water when heated; sulfur is a raw material for sulfur concrete. My pick for the first ISRU (in-situ resource) pilot plant.

sites.title: Groundwater record: boxwork ridges
sites.why: Ridge (clay) and hollow (carbonate) drill sites ~10 m apart record long-lived groundwater high on Mount Sharp. Best place for crew sampling: a one-day EVA covers what the rover needed months for.

sites.title: Steep Mount Sharp flank: avoid on foot
sites.why: Steepest ~500 m patch within 3 km of the boxwork site: mean slope 25° on the HiRISE DEM. Route crews along the valley floors Curiosity used.

sulfur.title: Gediz Vallis: field of pure sulfur stones
sulfur.found: 30 May 2024: a rock crushed by the wheels ("Convict Lake") showed yellow crystals of elemental sulfur, the first pure sulfur ever found on Mars. A whole field of similar bright, hand-sized stones lies around it.
sulfur.use: Direct binder for sulfur concrete: melt and mix, no chemical processing. The best sulfur site known on Mars.

sulfur.title: Sulfate-bearing unit: Mg- and Ca-sulfates
sulfur.found: Oct 2022: Curiosity entered the "sulfate-bearing unit" seen from orbit by MRO and found magnesium sulfate, calcium sulfate (incl. gypsum) and table salt. Drill sample "Canaima" (sol 3612).
sulfur.use: Large-volume sulfur ore. Sulfate must be reduced to elemental sulfur (energy-hungry), but it also releases water.

sulfur.title: Bagnold dunes: Gobabeb (Namib Dune)
sulfur.found: Jan 2016: first close-up study of an active dune on another planet. Basaltic sand scooped and sieved (<150 µm and 150 µm–1 mm fractions).
sulfur.use: Ready-sorted, loose aggregate under 1 mm: exactly the grain size used in the strongest sulfur-concrete mix. No crushing needed.

sulfur.title: Rocknest: wind-blown sand shadow
sulfur.found: Oct–Nov 2012: first scooped sample of the mission, five scoops of dust-coated sand from a sand shadow; the best-characterised Martian soil (CheMin + SAM).
sulfur.use: Well-known reference regolith 600 m from the landing site: fine aggregate for the first test batches.

events.title: Landing: Columbia Memorial Station
events.text: 4 Jan 2004. Spirit lands on the basaltic plains of Gusev crater.

events.title: Bonneville crater rim
events.text: Mar 2004. The ~200 m crater shows no lake sediments; the team turns east toward the hills.

events.title: Arrival at the Columbia Hills
events.text: Jun 2004. After a ~3 km drive, Spirit starts climbing West Spur and Husband Hill.

events.title: Comanche outcrop: carbonates
events.text: 2005 (identified 2010). Carbonate-rich rocks form in wet, non-acidic water.

events.title: Home Plate: almost pure silica
events.text: 2007. A dragging wheel exposes soil with up to ~90% silica, typical of hot springs or fumaroles. Strong evidence for a hydrothermal environment.

events.title: Troy: stuck in soft soil
events.text: 1 May 2009. Wheels break through a crust into sulfate-rich sand. Spirit becomes a stationary station; last contact 22 Mar 2010.

sites.title: Home Plate: hydrothermal silica
sites.why: Ancient hot-spring or fumarole deposits are among the best places on Mars to look for preserved biosignatures. Top astrobiology target for a crew.

sites.title: Troy: soft sulfate sand, no-go zone
sites.why: A thin crust over loose ferric-sulfate sand trapped Spirit for good. Keep crewed rovers out of the ~50 m bright-soil patch; the Spirit rover itself is a heritage site here.

sites.title: Sulfate-rich soils: water source
sites.why: The bright soils Spirit churned up near Home Plate are rich in hydrated sulfates. Low-temperature heating can release bound water. Excavate the margins, not the trap.

sites.title: Winter power: north-facing slope
sites.why: At ~14.6°S, Spirit survived winters by parking on north-tilted slopes facing the Sun (3rd winter on Home Plate's north edge). Selected from the DEM: a 8–20° north-facing slope next to Home Plate for solar arrays.

sites.title: Husband Hill: lookout & relay mast
sites.why: The highest point Spirit reached (summit, Aug 2005). Line of sight across the plains to the landing zone: a natural place for a comms relay and weather mast.

sulfur.title: Paso Robles: sulfate-rich bright soil
sulfur.found: Feb 2005: Spirit's wheels dug up light-toned soil with >30 wt% SO3: ferric, Mg- and Ca-sulfates plus phosphate. The most sulfur-rich material Spirit found.
sulfur.use: Richest sulfate ore in Gusev; loose, so it needs no drilling. Reduce to sulfur for the binder.
sulfur.src: Lane et al. 2008; Ming et al. 2006

sulfur.title: Arad: sulfate soil
sulfur.found: Sol 721: second large exposure of light-toned, hydrated ferric-sulfate soil, south of Husband Hill.
sulfur.use: Secondary sulfate source on the route to Home Plate.

sulfur.title: Tyrone: sulfate soil near Home Plate
sulfur.found: Sol 790: third major exposure of ferric-sulfate soil; so loose that several sols were needed to free the rover.
sulfur.use: Sulfate source, but soft ground: excavate from the edge, do not drive in. Troy (where Spirit was trapped for good) is the same kind of soil.

sulfur.title: Gusev plains basaltic soil
sulfur.found: Sols 113–115: "Big Hole" trench on the basaltic plains, ~9 cm deep, analysed with APXS and Mössbauer.
sulfur.use: Uniform basaltic soil across the flat plains: easy, safe aggregate source near a landing zone.

events.title: Landing: Octavia E. Butler Landing
events.text: 18 Feb 2021. Perseverance lands on the floor of Jezero crater, a 45 km basin that once held a lake fed by a river delta.

events.title: Ingenuity: first powered flight on another planet
events.text: 19 Apr 2021. The 1.8 kg helicopter lifts off from "Wright Brothers Field".

events.title: First rock core: "Rochette"
events.text: Sep 2021. The first sample sealed for a possible return to Earth.

events.title: Arrival at the delta front
events.text: Apr 2022. The rover reaches the layered sediments of the ancient river delta.

events.title: Ingenuity's last flight (#72)
events.text: Jan 2024. After 72 flights a damaged rotor ends the mission; the helicopter stays here as a weather and test station.

events.title: Cheyava Falls: potential biosignature
events.text: 21 Jul 2024. Core "Sapphire Canyon" from a leopard-spotted mudstone in Neretva Vallis. Published Sep 2025 as the best candidate so far for signs of ancient microbial life.

events.title: Climbing out of the crater
events.text: Dec 2024. Perseverance climbs the crater rim to reach some of the oldest rocks it has seen.

events.title: Today: latest position
events.text: Last reported drive, sol 2022 (NASA MMGIS feed).

sites.title: Cheyava Falls: return for the biosignature
sites.why: The strongest candidate yet for signs of ancient life. A crew with a field lab can sample the whole outcrop and test it in-situ, instead of waiting for sample return.

sites.title: Delta mudstones & carbonates: water source
sites.why: Clay- and carbonate-bearing delta sediments hold bound water. Close to a flat crater floor for a processing plant.

sites.title: Ingenuity: first Mars aircraft
sites.why: Heritage site: the first aircraft on another world. Inspect the blades and electronics to learn how they fail after years of cold, dust and UV. Valuable for future crewed drones.

sites.title: Steepest slopes in view: crater rim / delta scarp
sites.why: Steepest ~500 m patch on the DEM (mean 22°). Route crews around delta scarps and the rim.

sulfur.title: Hogwallow Flats: sulfate-cemented siltstone
sulfur.found: Jun–Aug 2022: fine-grained delta rocks cemented by hydrated sulfate; cores "Hazeltop" and "Bearwallow" (sols 509, 516).
sulfur.use: Sulfate ore at the foot of the delta, next to flat crater floor for a processing plant.
sulfur.src: Williams et al. LPSC 2023; Stack Morgan et al. GSA 2022

sulfur.title: Yori Pass / Hidden Harbor: Fe-Mg sulfates
sulfur.found: Nov 2022: lateral equivalent of Hogwallow Flats; PIXL found abundant Fe-Mg sulfates and clays. Core "Kukaklek" (sol 631).
sulfur.use: Second sulfate outcrop ~500 m from Hogwallow Flats: two ore faces close together.

sulfur.title: Observation Mountain: regolith samples
sulfur.found: 2 and 7 Dec 2022: first regolith samples, "Atmo Mountain" and "Crosswind Lake", from a wind-blown megaripple of mixed sand and dust.
sulfur.use: Proven, sampled aggregate right next to the sulfate outcrops: binder ore and aggregate within ~100 m.
sulfur.src: NASA sample table; Simon et al. 2025, PNAS
